interactions.summary: Jiang keeps pressing for the reason Dante takes the long route, and a student answers that poetry works through emotional or original thinking rather than straight logical statement.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang-led classroom exchange with one student answer

interactions.summary: Jiang reframes the issue as a historical and imaginative challenge: could Dante in 1321 have foreseen a multilingual group in Beijing discussing his intentions in 2026?

Students answer Jiang's Dante-in-2026 thought experiment by arguing that great writers expect lasting remembrance, truth survives the test of time, and Dante's visionary journey and vernacular ambition may have been aimed at a far larger future readership.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Jiang-led classroom exchange with multiple student answers

claims.claim: Jiang asks whether Dante in 1321 could have imagined that a multilingual group in Beijing would be discussing the Divine Comedy in 2026, turning literary interpretation into a question about truth surviving across centuries and cultures.
claims.temporal_scope: Jiang question posed on 2026-06-15 about Dante's 1321 authorship and the class's 2026 setting.

claims.claim: A student suggests that poets do not always proceed logically and instead work through emotional or original thinking, though the answer is noisy and only loosely formulated.
One student says Dante could have anticipated enduring readership in a general sense because writers hope their words will be remembered as masterpieces long after them.
Another student argues that if a work is close to what is true, it can withstand the test of time whether the horizon is fifty years or two thousand years.
Jiang accepts the previous line of thought as a good answer and re-asks whether Dante could have known that future readers in Beijing would still be reading him.
A student speculates that Dante may have somehow seen this future audience on his journey and points to his decision to write in the vernacular as part of why the work could travel to more people.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang forces the room to imagine Dante in 1321 somehow reaching a multilingual Beijing classroom in 2026.
signature_moments.source_phrase: could he possibly imagine that in the year 2026, that we would be in Beijing
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This expands the packet from local pedagogy to the question of what kind of writing can outlive its world and address strangers centuries later.

signature_moments.moment: Truth is proposed as the thing that survives fifty years, a thousand years, or two thousand years.
signature_moments.source_phrase: if what he writes is close to the truth
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It condenses the class's strongest answer into a criterion for literary endurance that will matter for the later read.

signature_moments.moment: Dante's vernacular choice is pulled into the conversation as part of how the poem reaches beyond its own age.
signature_moments.source_phrase: leaving this work in, for example, in vernacular
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves a concrete mechanism by which the class links literary form to transhistorical reach.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The student's phrase for how truth-bearing writing remains legible across very long stretches of history.
Raised by a student as part of why Dante's work could circulate beyond elite or local audiences.
A student's rough phrase for poetic thinking that does not move by straightforward logic.

chronology_notes.note: This packet makes chronology explicit inside the lecture by juxtaposing Dante's 1321 authorship with the class's 2026 Beijing setting; it does not revise Jiang's dated position across sources.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's answer is partly noisy and includes a muddled Elon Musk aside, so only the broad contrast between poetic originality and strict logic is stable.
